analysis.one_liner: Funds the IRS to audit the wealthiest households and largest corporations at set minimum rates and improve taxpayer services.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the House Appropriations Committee without a vote, despite 31 Democratic sponsors and cosponsors and no Republican support.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have added roughly $11.8 billion a year for ten years to the IRS: $5 billion for enforcement staff and audits, $4.3 billion for technology and fraud protection, and $2.5 billion for taxpayer services. It would have required the IRS to audit a share of the highest incomes every year — 50% of returns with $100 million or more in income, for example, and 90% of the largest corporations. Its findings cite a tax gap of roughly $381 billion a year in unpaid taxes, with an estimated 70% coming from the top 1% of earners.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers who pay what they owe, because fewer people would successfully avoid paying taxes they legally owe — the bill's findings cite an average annual 'surtax' of more than $3,000 per household to cover unpaid taxes. Taxpayers who need help filing or resolving account problems would also gain from more IRS customer-service staff. Wealthy households and large corporations would see more of their returns examined.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers who pay what they owe

how_it_helps.text: Appropriates $5 billion a year for ten years (FY2022–FY2031) for IRS enforcement, including staff to raise audit rates and to pursue criminal tax and financial-crime cases.

Sets statutory minimum audit levels aimed at the top of the income scale: 50% of returns with income of $100 million or more, 35% at $10–100 million, 20% at $5–10 million, 10% at $1–5 million, and 90% of corporations with gross income of $20 billion or more.
Appropriates $3.8 billion a year for IRS operations support (protecting taxpayer data and reducing tax-related theft and fraud) and $500 million a year for technology modernization.
Appropriates $2.5 billion a year for taxpayer services, adding staff for filing help, pre-filing assistance, and account services.

The bill's findings cite CBO estimates that each additional dollar spent on tax enforcement could yield more than $4 in revenue, and that $40 billion of added enforcement funding over ten years would raise $103 billion.

analysis.who_pays: High-income households and large corporations would pay more of the taxes they currently avoid, through higher audit rates. All taxpayers, as a group, would bear the added federal spending of roughly $11.8 billion a year, offset in part by the revenue the added enforcement is projected to recover.
analysis.who_pays_short: Wealthy filers, big corporations, and taxpayers generally

drawbacks.text: The bill appropriates the money as a set amount each year, outside the normal annual appropriations process, which reduces Congress's flexibility to adjust IRS funding as conditions change.

The audit-rate floors are set in law by income and gross income brackets, which would apply rigidly regardless of case quality; returns with $1 million or more in income include many owners of profitable small and mid-sized businesses, not only the very wealthy, so some pass-through business owners would face audit rates of 10–35%.

Revenue projections from added enforcement spending are uncertain; the bill's own findings acknowledge a range (CBO estimated $61 billion of revenue from a $20 billion funding increase versus $103 billion from $40 billion), meaning the added spending might not fully pay for itself.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The stated math favors the bill: the findings cite a $381 billion annual tax gap concentrated among top earners, audit rates that fell roughly by half over a decade, and CBO estimates that enforcement dollars return several times their cost. The honest objections are design, not direction: rigid statutory audit floors and ten-year appropriations outside the annual budget process reduce flexibility, and revenue gains are projections, not guarantees. On balance, a genuine attempt to make high earners and large corporations pay taxes they already legally owe, with real but manageable design flaws.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in February 2021 and sent to the House Appropriations Committee, which never acted on it, so it never got a committee vote or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter DeFazio introduced the bill on February 18, 2021, joined by 24 original cosponsors, all House Democrats.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Appropriations.

No further action was ever taken on the bill; the action history ends with the referral to committee, and the bill never received a markup, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
The bill eventually listed 30 cosponsors, all Democrats; no House Republican cosponsored it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-income households and large corporations that would have faced the mandated audit-rate increases are better off because the bill died, as are anyone opposed to the added federal spending. Ordinary taxpayers who pay what they owe are worse off, continuing to cover an estimated $381 billion-a-year tax gap that the bill's findings say falls on them as an average of more than $3,000 per household per year.

for.name: Rep. Peter DeFazio
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its sponsorship.

for.name: 30 of 213 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.

against.name: House Committee on Appropriations
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Rep. Rosa DeLauro, D-CT)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee action, leaving it without a markup, a vote, or a report to the floor for the entire two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and all 30 cosponsors were House Democrats, and no Republican signed on; because the bill never reached a vote, no recorded roll-call split exists.

industries.industry: High-income households (roughly $1 million+ in annual income)
industries.note: The bill would mandate audit rates of 10% to 50% for returns with $1 million or more in income, versus roughly 3.2% for millionaires in 2018, and the bill's findings estimate 70% of the tax gap comes from the top 1%. Their gain from the bill's failure is avoiding taxes they legally owe, which the bill says costs other households an average of $3,000 a year.

industries.industry: Largest corporations ($1 billion+ in gross income)
industries.note: Audit floors of 50% for corporations over $1 billion in gross income and 90% for those over $20 billion would reverse a decade of declining corporate audit rates, which the bill says fell from over 90% to about 50% for the largest corporations.

More audits and expanded taxpayer services would mean more representation, audit defense, and filing work for the industry, though large accounting firms advising the biggest corporate clients would also face more scrutiny of aggressive positions.
